category: Core vocabulary: pets and animal care

entries.meaning: The branch of medicine that deals with animal health. ---
examples: He went into veterinary medicine after college.
The school of veterinary medicine is on the north campus.
Veterinary medicine has changed a lot in twenty years.

entries.meaning: A clinic where sick or injured animals are treated. ---
examples: There's a 24-hour animal hospital off the highway.
We rushed her to the animal hospital at midnight.
Both animal hospitals were closed on Sunday.

entries.meaning: Food made for animals kept at home. ---
examples: Pet food has gotten expensive.
We buy pet food in bulk twice a year.
The recall covered several brands of pet food.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: say a bag of pet food, never 'a pet food'.

entries.meaning: Food made for dogs. ---
examples: We're out of dog food again.
She mixes wet dog food into his kibble.
A bag of dog food costs thirty dollars now.

entries.meaning: Food made for cats. ---
examples: The cat food is under the sink.
He opened a can of cat food and she came running.
Pick up some cat food while you're out.

entries.meaning: Dry pet food shaped into small hard pieces. ---
examples: He gets a cup of kibble twice a day.
The puppy won't touch dry kibble.
There's kibble all over the kitchen floor.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: a cup of kibble, not 'a kibble'.

entries.meaning: A small piece of tasty food given to an animal as a reward. ---
examples: Give him a treat when he sits.
She keeps treats in her coat pocket.
One more treat and that's it for tonight.

entries.meaning: A tough toy made for a dog to bite and chew on. ---
examples: The puppy destroyed his new chew toy in an hour.
Get her a rubber chew toy instead of a shoe.
There are chew toys under every couch cushion.

entries.meaning: A strap or cord clipped to a collar to keep a dog under control. ---
examples: Keep your dog on a leash in the park.
He grabbed the leash and the dog went crazy.
Both leashes were tangled together.
entries.contrast: American leash; the British say lead.

entries.meaning: A small metal disc on a collar with the owner's contact details. ---
examples: His dog tag has our phone number on it.
The dog tag jingles whenever he moves.
Order two dog tags in case one falls off.
entries.contrast: Dog tags is also the everyday name for the metal ID tags a US soldier wears.

entries.meaning: A small shelter outdoors for a dog to sleep in. ---
examples: He built a doghouse out of scrap lumber.
The old doghouse is falling apart.
Both doghouses need new roofs.
entries.contrast: American doghouse is the British kennel; 'in the doghouse' also means in trouble with someone.

entries.meaning: Absorbent grains poured into a tray for a cat to use. ---
examples: Pick up a bag of cat litter.
Cat litter tracks all over the house.
This cat litter is supposed to control odor.

entries.meaning: A covered upright post a cat can dig its claws into. ---
examples: She sharpens her claws on the scratching post.
Get him a scratching post before he ruins the couch.
We have scratching posts in two rooms.

entries.meaning: A tall carpeted structure with platforms for a cat to climb and sleep on. ---
examples: The gray cat sleeps on top of the cat tree.
We put the cat tree by the window.
Those cat trees are surprisingly expensive.

entries.meaning: A minty herb whose smell excites most cats. ---
examples: A little catnip makes him roll around like a kitten.
The toy is stuffed with dried catnip.
Catnip has no effect on some cats at all.

entries.meaning: Dried flakes or pellets fed to fish in a tank. ---
examples: Sprinkle a little fish food on the surface.
We're almost out of fish food.
Too much fish food fouls the water.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is washing and trimming pets. ---
examples: Our groomer cut his nails too short.
She works as a dog groomer downtown.
The groomers are booked through the holidays.

entries.meaning: The natural loss of hair from an animal's coat. ---
examples: Shedding gets worse in the spring.
This brush cuts down on shedding.
There's no way to stop the shedding completely.

entries.meaning: Tiny flakes of skin from an animal that often cause allergies. ---
examples: My sister is allergic to cat dander.
Dander collects in the carpet.
An air filter helps with pet dander.

entries.meaning: A wad of swallowed hair that a cat coughs up. ---
examples: The cat coughed up a hairball on the rug.
Hairballs are common in long-haired breeds.
There's special food that prevents hairballs.

entries.meaning: A collar treated with chemicals that kill fleas. ---
examples: We put a flea collar on both dogs.
The flea collar smells awful.
Flea collars work for about six months.

entries.meaning: A medicine put on an animal to kill or keep off fleas. ---
examples: The vet recommended a monthly flea treatment.
She applies the flea treatment between his shoulder blades.
Some flea treatments kill ticks too.

entries.meaning: Treating an animal with medicine that kills intestinal worms. ---
examples: The puppy is due for deworming.
Deworming is part of the first vet visit.
Regular deworming keeps the whole litter healthy.

entries.meaning: An operation that makes a female animal unable to have young. ---
examples: The shelter covers the cost of spaying.
Spaying is usually done before six months.
She scheduled the spaying for next week.

entries.meaning: An operation that makes a male animal unable to father young. ---
examples: Neutering calmed him down a lot.
The clinic offers low-cost neutering.
They require neutering before adoption.
entries.contrast: Americans say NOO-tur-ing; the British say NYOO-tur-ing.

entries.meaning: Surgically removing a cat's claws. ---
examples: Declawing is banned in several cities.
Most vets refuse to do declawing now.
She chose nail caps instead of declawing.

entries.meaning: A repeat injection that keeps an earlier vaccine working. ---
examples: He's due for a booster shot in March.
The booster shot costs about forty dollars.
Puppies need several booster shots the first year.

entries.meaning: A contagious dog illness that causes a harsh, dry cough. ---
examples: The whole shelter came down with kennel cough.
Kennel cough sounds like a honking goose.
He caught kennel cough at doggy daycare.
entries.contrast: The gh in cough sounds like f: KAWF.

entries.meaning: A serious viral disease of dogs and some other animals. ---
examples: The puppy was vaccinated against distemper.
Distemper is often fatal in young dogs.
The shelter had an outbreak of distemper last winter.

entries.meaning: A skin disease caused by mites that makes an animal's hair fall out. ---
examples: The stray had mange on his back and ears.
Mange is caused by tiny mites burrowing in the skin.
Medicated baths cleared up the mange.

entries.meaning: A contagious skin infection that leaves round bald patches. ---
examples: The kitten came home with ringworm.
Ringworm spreads to people, so wash your hands.
It took a month to get rid of the ringworm.
entries.contrast: Ringworm is a fungus, not a worm.

entries.meaning: A parasitic worm carried by mosquitoes that lives in a dog's heart and lungs. ---
examples: Give him the heartworm pill on the first of the month.
The dog tested positive for heartworm.
Heartworms can grow up to a foot long.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Countable for the worms themselves; uncountable for the disease: tested positive for heartworm.

entries.meaning: Painlessly ending the life of a hopelessly sick animal. ---
examples: The vet talked us through euthanasia.
Euthanasia is never an easy decision.
The clinic charges separately for euthanasia.

entries.meaning: A policy that pays part of an animal's medical bills. ---
examples: We finally bought pet insurance.
Pet insurance covered most of the surgery.
Read what the pet insurance actually pays for.

entries.meaning: The city department that picks up stray and dangerous animals. ---
examples: Somebody called animal control about the loose dog.
Animal control picked up the raccoon in our attic.
Animal control holds strays for two weeks.

entries.meaning: The good treatment and comfort of animals. ---
examples: She volunteers for an animal welfare group.
The law raised animal welfare standards on farms.
Animal welfare was the main issue in the campaign.

entries.meaning: A place that takes in homeless animals and finds homes for them. ---
examples: We adopted him from the animal shelter.
The animal shelter is full again.
Both animal shelters need foster homes.

entries.meaning: A charity that rescues animals and works against cruelty to them. ---
examples: The humane society runs a low-cost clinic.
She donates to the local humane society every year.
Several humane societies took in animals after the fire.
entries.contrast: Humane is stressed on the second syllable, hyoo-MAYN, unlike human.

entries.meaning: A long-handled scoop for picking up dog waste. ---
examples: Bring a pooper scooper to the dog park.
He keeps a pooper scooper in the trunk.
The park provides bags but no pooper scoopers.

entries.meaning: A small plastic bag for picking up after a dog. ---
examples: Take a poop bag with you.
The dispenser was out of poop bags.
She tied the poop bag shut and dropped it in the can.

entries.meaning: A fenced public area where dogs can run without a leash. ---
examples: We take him to the dog park every morning.
The dog park has a separate side for small dogs.
There are three dog parks in the city.

entries.meaning: Someone paid to take other people's dogs out for walks. ---
examples: We hired a dog walker for weekday afternoons.
The dog walker handles six dogs at once.
Good dog walkers book up fast.
entries.contrast: The l in walker is silent: WAW-kur.

entries.meaning: Someone paid to look after an animal while its owner is away. ---
examples: A pet sitter stays at the house while we travel.
Our pet sitter sends photos every day.
She works weekends as a pet sitter.

entries.meaning: A business that looks after dogs during the working day. ---
examples: He goes to doggy daycare three days a week.
The doggy daycare has a webcam.
There are two doggy daycares near the office.

entries.meaning: An animal's readiness to do what it is told. ---
examples: The dog has no obedience at all.
We're working on basic obedience.
Obedience takes daily practice.
entries.contrast: Stressed on the second syllable: oh-BEE-dee-uhns.

entries.meaning: A class where dogs are taught to follow commands. ---
examples: We sent the puppy to obedience school.
Obedience school meets on Tuesday nights.
Both obedience schools had waiting lists.

entries.meaning: Teaching a young animal to relieve itself outdoors. ---
examples: Housebreaking a puppy takes patience.
We're still in the middle of housebreaking.
Crate training helps with housebreaking.
entries.contrast: In legal English housebreaking means breaking into a house; the pet sense is a separate word.

entries.meaning: A game in which a dog runs after a thrown object and brings it back. ---
examples: He'll play fetch until he collapses.
We threw the ball and played fetch for an hour.
Fetch is the only game she cares about.

entries.meaning: A whistle pitched so high that dogs hear it and people barely do. ---
examples: The trainer blew a dog whistle we couldn't hear.
He carries a dog whistle on his key ring.
Dog whistles work above the range of human hearing.
entries.contrast: The t in whistle is silent: WIS-uhl. In politics a dog whistle is also a coded message.

entries.meaning: A person who keeps an animal at home. ---
examples: Every pet owner on the block got the notice.
Pet owners have to clean up after their dogs.
As a pet owner, you're responsible for the vaccinations.

entries.meaning: A person who controls and works with a trained animal. ---
examples: The handler led the dog around the ring.
Police dogs live with their handlers.
She's been a handler at dog shows for years.

entries.meaning: A competition where dogs are judged against their breed standard. ---
examples: They won best in breed at the dog show.
The dog show is at the fairgrounds this weekend.
He judges dog shows around the country.

entries.meaning: A place that breeds puppies for profit in bad conditions. ---
examples: The dogs were rescued from a puppy mill.
Never buy from a puppy mill.
The state shut down two puppy mills last year.

entries.meaning: The keeping of animals so that they produce young. ---
examples: Breeding season starts in the spring.
She retired the mare from breeding.
Careful breeding reduces hereditary disease.

entries.meaning: An animal whose parents are both of the same breed. ---
examples: He's a purebred, with papers and everything.
Purebreds often cost thousands of dollars.
The shelter had one purebred among forty mutts.

entries.meaning: An animal whose parents are of two different breeds. ---
examples: The dog is a crossbreed of a poodle and a lab.
Crossbreeds are often healthier than purebreds.
That crossbreed got the best of both breeds.
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, KRAWSS-breed; as a verb the stress moves to the second.

entries.meaning: A dog of no particular breed. ---
examples: He's just a mutt from the pound.
Mutts make great family dogs.
Our mutt is part shepherd and part who knows what.

entries.meaning: A dog of mixed and unknown breeding. ---
examples: The old mongrel followed us home.
Mongrels were once looked down on at shows.
She adopted a scruffy brown mongrel.

entries.meaning: A written record of an animal's ancestors. ---
examples: The breeder showed us the puppy's pedigree.
His pedigree goes back four generations.
Pedigrees are registered with the kennel club.

entries.meaning: The smallest and weakest animal in a litter. ---
examples: The runt of the litter is always the smallest.
Nobody wanted the runt, so we took him.
Runts often need extra feeding at first.

entries.meaning: Any of several small, bold breeds of dog bred to hunt animals in burrows. ---
examples: That terrier barks at everything.
Terriers were bred to hunt rats.
She has a wire-haired terrier.

entries.meaning: Retriever has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A golden retriever is good with kids.
The retriever brought the stick right back.
Retrievers love the water.
The retriever swam out and brought back both ducks.
Retrievers love cold water more than any other breed.
Their black retriever is twelve years old and still works.

senses.head: A breed of gundog trained to bring back shot birds
examples: A golden retriever is good with kids.
The retriever brought the stick right back.
Retrievers love the water.

senses.head: A dog trained to bring back birds that a hunter has shot
examples: The retriever swam out and brought back both ducks.
Retrievers love cold water more than any other breed.
Their black retriever is twelve years old and still works.

entries.meaning: A breed of dog with thick curly hair, often clipped in patterns. ---
examples: Her poodle just came back from the groomer.
Poodles don't shed much.
The standard poodle is much bigger than the toy.

entries.meaning: A heavy short-legged breed with a wide flat face. ---
examples: The bulldog snores louder than my father.
Bulldogs overheat easily in summer.
He walks a stocky brown bulldog every evening.

entries.meaning: A small hunting hound with drooping ears and a loud bark. ---
examples: The beagle followed the scent across the yard.
Beagles have a loud, carrying bark.
We named the beagle after a cartoon dog.

entries.meaning: A breed of long-nosed sheepdog with a thick coat. ---
examples: The collie herded the kids into the corner.
Collies need a job to do.
A border collie is the smartest dog I've owned.

entries.meaning: A breed of dog with a long body and very short legs. ---
examples: The dachshund can't handle stairs anymore.
Dachshunds were bred to hunt badgers.
Their dachshund is shaped like a hot dog.
entries.contrast: A German loanword: DAHKS-huund. Many Americans just say wiener dog.

entries.meaning: A small breed of dog with a flat wrinkled face and a curled tail. ---
examples: The pug wheezes when he gets excited.
Pugs have a lot of breathing problems.
She dressed the pug in a sweater.

entries.meaning: A thick-coated northern breed bred to pull sleds. ---
examples: A husky needs cold weather and a lot of running.
Huskies howl instead of barking.
The husky has one blue eye and one brown.
entries.contrast: Also an adjective meaning big and sturdy, or a voice that sounds rough.

entries.meaning: A tall, very fast breed of dog with a narrow body. ---
examples: The greyhound can outrun a bicycle.
Retired racing greyhounds make calm pets.
The greyhound sleeps twenty hours a day.

entries.meaning: A breed of dog with long silky ears and a wavy coat. ---
examples: The spaniel has long, silky ears.
Spaniels were bred to flush birds out of cover.
Their cocker spaniel is nine years old.

entries.meaning: A small herding breed with short legs and large upright ears. ---
examples: The corgi has short legs and no patience.
Corgis shed constantly.
She posts pictures of her corgi every day.

entries.meaning: A large hound with a superb sense of smell, used for tracking. ---
examples: The bloodhound tracked him three miles.
Bloodhounds have the best noses of any breed.
Police brought in a bloodhound.
entries.contrast: Blood is pronounced BLUHD, rhyming with mud.

entries.meaning: A small dog kept purely as company. ---
examples: The little lapdog never leaves her side.
Lapdogs were bred for company, not work.
He's a sixty-pound lapdog in his own mind.

entries.meaning: A dog kept to bark a warning when strangers come. ---
examples: They keep a watchdog at the lot.
Watchdogs bark at anything that moves.
The watchdog woke the whole street.
entries.contrast: A watchdog is also a group that keeps an eye on a government or an industry.

entries.meaning: A dog trained to protect a place or a person. ---
examples: A guard dog patrols the warehouse at night.
Guard dogs are trained not to take food from strangers.
The sign warns about a guard dog.

entries.meaning: A dog trained to lead a blind person safely. ---
examples: His guide dog is a yellow lab.
Guide dogs are allowed in restaurants.
The guide dog stopped at the curb.

entries.meaning: A dog trained to do specific tasks for a person with a disability. ---
examples: Her service dog wears a vest in public.
Service dogs can go anywhere their handler goes.
Don't pet a service dog while it's working.

entries.meaning: A dog bred and trained to pull a sled over snow. ---
examples: Sled dogs can run a hundred miles a day.
Each sled dog eats an enormous amount.
The sled dog team pulled up the trail.

entries.meaning: An adult male cat. ---
examples: A big orange tomcat lives under the porch.
Tomcats fight over territory.
The tomcat has a torn ear.

entries.meaning: An affectionate word for a cat, especially a young one. ---
examples: Come here, kitty.
The kids named the kitty Waffles.
Two kitties were curled up in the box.

entries.meaning: A friendly, informal word for a dog. ---
examples: That pooch has the run of the house.
Take the pooch out before bed.
A couple of pooches were waiting outside the store.

entries.meaning: A cat with a striped or blotched coat. ---
examples: The orange tabby sleeps in the window.
Tabbies have an M-shaped mark on the forehead.
We adopted a gray tabby from the shelter.

entries.meaning: A cat that lives wild and avoids people. ---
examples: A colony of feral cats lives behind the diner.
The feral cat won't let anyone near her.
Volunteers trap and neuter feral cats.

entries.meaning: A cat, or any animal of the cat family. ---
examples: The clinic treats both canines and felines.
A feline landed silently on the fence.
Felines sleep most of the day.

entries.meaning: A dog, or any animal of the dog family. ---
examples: The vaccine protects canines against several viruses.
This unit works with a canine partner.
Canines and felines need different diets.
entries.contrast: Canine is also the name of the pointed tooth on each side of your front teeth.

entries.meaning: A tiny brightly colored tropical fish kept in tanks. ---
examples: The guppies had babies again.
A single guppy costs about two dollars.
Guppies are a good fish for a first tank.

entries.meaning: A small desert rodent with long back legs, kept as a pet. ---
examples: The gerbil runs on his wheel all night.
Gerbils need deep bedding to dig in.
Her class keeps a gerbil in the corner.
entries.contrast: The g sounds like j: JUR-buhl.

entries.meaning: A small South American rodent with extremely soft gray fur. ---
examples: A chinchilla has the softest fur of any animal.
Chinchillas bathe in dust, not water.
The chinchilla chewed through the cage bars.

entries.meaning: A small gray Australian parrot with a crest and orange cheek patches. ---
examples: The cockatiel whistles the same three notes all day.
Cockatiels can learn to talk a little.
Her cockatiel rides around on her shoulder.

entries.meaning: The branch of farming that deals with raising and caring for livestock. ---
examples: He studied animal husbandry at the state college.
Animal husbandry covers feeding, breeding, and health.
The course includes basic animal husbandry.
entries.contrast: Husbandry here has nothing to do with husbands; it means the care of farm animals.

entries.meaning: The coming together of a male and female animal to produce young. ---
examples: Mating usually happens in early spring.
The pair were kept apart until mating season.
He wrote down the date of mating.

entries.meaning: The time an animal carries its young before birth. ---
examples: Gestation in dogs is about nine weeks.
The cow is in the last month of gestation.
Gestation is shorter in smaller animals.

entries.meaning: Driving and keeping together a group of animals. ---
examples: Herding is pure instinct for these dogs.
The border collie is bred for herding.
Herding the cattle downhill took all day.

entries.meaning: A male horse that has been castrated. ---
examples: She rides a bay gelding.
Geldings are usually calmer than stallions.
The gelding is fifteen years old.

entries.meaning: An animal between one and two years old. ---
examples: The yearling is already taller than its mother.
Yearlings sell well at this auction.
He bought a yearling colt.

entries.meaning: A worker who feeds horses and cleans out a stable. ---
examples: The stable hand feeds the horses at six.
He worked as a stable hand through high school.
Two stable hands muck out the barn each day.

entries.meaning: A curved iron plate nailed to the bottom of a horse's hoof. ---
examples: The horseshoe had worked loose.
Horseshoes are nailed into the hard part of the hoof.
She hung a horseshoe over the door for luck.

entries.meaning: A craftsman who trims horses' hooves and fits their shoes. ---
examples: The farrier comes out every six weeks.
A good farrier is hard to find.
Farriers trim hooves as well as fit shoes.

entries.meaning: The straps around a horse's head that the reins attach to. ---
examples: He slipped the bridle over the horse's head.
The bridle hangs by the stall door.
All the bridles need oiling.
entries.contrast: Bridle sounds exactly like bridal, which means having to do with a wedding.

entries.meaning: A long strap running from the bridle that the rider holds to steer. ---
examples: She pulled on the left rein.
Hold the reins in both hands.
One rein had snapped clean through.
entries.contrast: Rein sounds like rain and like reign — three different words.

entries.meaning: One of the two metal loops hanging from a saddle for the rider's feet. ---
examples: His boot slipped out of the stirrup.
Shorten the stirrups before you mount.
One stirrup hangs lower than the other.

entries.meaning: A small metal point on a rider's heel, used to urge a horse on. ---
examples: The rider touched the horse with a spur.
Spurs should be used lightly, if at all.
One spur had come off in the dirt.

entries.meaning: The low steady sound a contented cat makes. ---
examples: The cat let out a low purr.
You could hear his purr across the room.
Her purrs got louder when I scratched her chin.

entries.meaning: The crying sound a cat makes. ---
examples: A thin meow came from under the porch.
She answered with a single meow.
The meows got louder around dinnertime.

entries.meaning: A low threatening sound made in the throat by an animal. ---
examples: A low growl came from behind the couch.
He gave a warning growl and backed away.
The growls stopped when she recognized me.

entries.meaning: A sharp sound like a long s, made by an angry cat or a snake. ---
examples: The cat backed away with a hiss.
That hiss means leave her alone.
There were hisses from both cats.

entries.meaning: A long loud cry made by a dog or wolf. ---
examples: A long howl woke the whole street.
The dog let out a mournful howl.
You could hear howls from the kennel.

entries.meaning: A high complaining sound made by a dog wanting something. ---
examples: The puppy let out a whine at the door.
That whine means he needs to go out.
We ignored the whines until morning.
entries.contrast: For most Americans whine sounds exactly like wine.

entries.meaning: A short sharp cry of pain or surprise from a dog. ---
examples: The dog gave a sharp yelp when I stepped on his tail.
A yelp came from the yard.
There were a couple of yelps, then silence.

entries.meaning: An angry growl made with the teeth showing. ---
examples: He curled his lip in a snarl.
The snarl was enough to back the stranger off.
Snarls came from both sides of the fence.

entries.meaning: A quick side-to-side movement of an animal's tail. ---
examples: He greeted us with a wag of his tail.
A slow wag means something different from a fast one.
Her tail gave a couple of wags.

entries.meaning: The long high call a horse makes. ---
examples: The horse let out a neigh.
A neigh carried across the field.
Neighs came from the far end of the barn.
entries.contrast: Sounds just like nay; the gh is silent.

entries.meaning: The deep call a cow makes.
examples: A long moo came from the barn.
The calf answered with a soft moo.
You could hear the moos at feeding time.
